newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech CPI hinges on social support deal - c.bank.
newsitem.headline: Czech CPI hinges on social support deal - c.bank.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB) said on Thursday it was watching the level of social support the government grants to offset energy and rent increases, before assessing effects of price deregulation on inflation.

"Up to now it is not quite clear how (energy and housing rent price rises) will work, because on one hand the issue of deregulation is not quite completed, and the other hand would be the question of any social balancing," CNB spokesman Martin Svehla told Reuters.

The three parties in the ruling centre-right coalition government have agreed to deregulate almost all state-controlled housing rents by 2000, and to allow an average 50 percent increase in rents from July 1 this year.
The coalition parties have also agreed to a rise in the value added tax (VAT) on electricity and natural gas to 22 percent from five percent, which would be effective on July 1.
But the cabinet on Wednesday postponed final approval on the agreements, as more discussion was needed on support for low-income households.

Svehla again said that the central bank's target for 1997 was to keep inflation below eight percent. Czech inflation stood at 7.4 percent, year-on-year, in January with February results expected next Monday.
When asked the central bank's inflation forecast should the proposed price rises take effect, Svehla said an answer was not possible until the level of social supports is determined.
"Generally speaking deregulation means to cut inflationary expectations. Generally it is a good thing. On the other hand the social solutions can affect inflation as well," Svehla said.
"Unfortunately we don't know what it will be."
He said that the rise in prices would be balanced by a corresponding reduction in consumption.

"In itself it will be an important element into the future for lowering the inflation rate. But on the other hand this will be accompanied by some social support. I don't know what this will be. It can, under some circumstances impact the inflation in the worse direction," Svehla said.
Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik estimated last week that the planned price deregulations would raise the end-1997 annual inflation rate to no more than 9.5 percent.
He did not say whether the effect of social supports was included in this estimate.
